extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, law & economics researchers, empirical legal researchers, patent litigators, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and interpreting empirical outcomes of patent litigation across industries and technologies, with attention to selection effects, dataset limitations, and industry-specific litigation incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection / representativeness of litigated patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The patents litigated to summary judgment, trial, or appellate decision may not be representative of all patents or even all litigated patents; there is a potential selection story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If litigated-to-judgment patents differ systematically by industry/technology, results reflect that subset only. The paper enumerates potential selection stories and treats these as alternate explanations that limit generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability to observe settled-case outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot measure outcomes in settled cases because the terms of settlement agreements are almost always confidential; a settlement does not have a meaningful outcome on a specific issue like definiteness or infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlements reflect the parties' collective judgment about merits, costs, and uncertainty rather than resolution of legal issues; this limits ability to infer doctrinal outcomes from observed settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset coverage and representativeness (scale metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a small fraction (estimated 1–2%) of issued patents are ever litigated; the study's dataset includes less than 10% of filed lawsuits in the study years and may be closer to 5% of filed lawsuits and well under 0.1% of all patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These coverage metrics constrain generalizability. Analysts must state what fraction of the universe their sample represents and caveat conclusions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-specific filtering through prosecution/litigation/licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: The filtering of patents through prosecution, litigation, and licensing systems leaves a small and technologically uneven group of patents that reach judgment; the filtering process itself may be technology specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret outcome distributions as potentially shaped by upstream and midstream selection mechanisms that vary by technology (e.g., prosecutorial claiming strategies, licensing markets, settlement norms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and definition of ‘interim wins’ as an evaluative metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Recorded a patent owner interim win when summary judgment was denied and there was no further resolution of the dispute at the time of coding; included accused infringer victories vacated and remanded by the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting interim wins as patentee wins changes win-rate calculations and narrows gaps across technologies, but may overstate definitive merits outcomes because many interim wins end in settlement or remain pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Priest–Klein fifty-percent win-rate benchmark
rubrics_metrics.description: Priest and Klein suggested tried cases should have a 50% plaintiff win rate; deviations can indicate selection effects or inapplicability of the strong Priest–Klein hypothesis to patent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare observed win rates across procedural stages (summary judgment, trial, appeal) to the 50% benchmark, but account for industry-specific incentives and other law-and-economics factors that cause deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-and-economics selection factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Deviations from 50% can be caused by asymmetric stakes, costs, risk profiles, agency costs, endowment effects, and other complicating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate these abstract factors into concrete litigation incentives (e.g., asymmetric stakes in pharma, cost asymmetries in software) when explaining observed selection patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmaceutical/Hatch–Waxman-specific litigation incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Pharmaceutical litigation under the Hatch–Waxman Act is distinct: branded patentees often have FDA-granted exclusivity before litigation; infringement typically cannot occur until FDA approval; large market shares and profits change settlement incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for ANDA process timing, potential for reverse payments, generic exclusivity incentives, and relative litigation cost vs potential profits when analyzing pharma case selection and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse-payment (pay-for-delay) settlements in pharma
rubrics_metrics.description: Branded drug companies sometimes pay generics to drop challenges (reverse payments); these settlements were common during the dataset period and may affect which cases go to judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that reverse payments can lead to settlements of potentially strong or weak challenges; antitrust scrutiny (e.g., FTC v. Actavis) affects prevalence and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-practicing-entity (NPE) dynamics in software litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are likely more NPE lawsuits in the software field; NPEs lack product-market relationships and typical settlement options (e.g., cross-licenses), and are unlikely to obtain injunctive relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that NPE incentives and settlement behavior differ from operating companies; evidence on NPE vs non-NPE settlement rates is mixed and may be confounded by sampling of repeat litigants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource asymmetry and number-of-defendants effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Large defendants in the computer industry may have more resources than smaller plaintiffs, and software cases may have more defendants, increasing the chance that at least one defendant maintains the case through summary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for defendants' resources and defendant count in models of case progression and selection to adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product architecture and design-around incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Products with many subcomponents (e.g., smartphones) make it easier to design around patents covering small components, which curtails damages and can raise defense costs relative to recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When damages are easily curtailed, parties have stronger incentives to settle; the 'cost-of-litigation defense' strategy may induce nuisance-value settlements regardless of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingent-fee representation effects on selection and settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Contingent-fee counsel reduce plaintiffs' upfront costs and influence settlement incentives; contingent-fee lawyers may either seek early settlements or screen for stronger cases—empirical effects unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model how fee arrangements change plaintiffs' willingness to litigate vs settle and consider potential screening effects of contingent-fee acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural posture: jury vs bench trial effects on summary judgment usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Pharmaceutical trials are almost all bench trials, while software, biotech, and mechanical are nearly all jury trials; courts may be less willing to grant summary judgment in cases without a jury demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include trial type as a covariate when analyzing the likelihood of summary judgment and case dispositions; absence/presence of prior summary judgment motions affects which cases reach trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis: per-patent vs per-lawsuit measurement choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Transforming the unit of analysis (e.g., from per-patent to per-lawsuit) affects conclusions; e.g., a per-lawsuit patentee victory is defined as at least one patent adjudicated valid and infringed in the suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about units of analysis and report robustness checks using alternate units (per-patent, per-claim, per-lawsuit) because counts and win-rates change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extralegal influences on judicial decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Media coverage and academic discourse (notably criticism of software patents) may influence judges directly or indirectly, potentially biasing outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge possible extralegal effects and consider controls or sensitivity analyses where feasible; cannot directly measure such influences in this dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrinal stability / concreteness varies by technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent law doctrines may be more or less concrete by technology (e.g., chemical patents had low rates of obviousness/indefiniteness in dataset), leading to different invalidity/indefiniteness rates across fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret cross-technology outcome differences partly as reflections of doctrinal uncertainty; adjust empirical models to account for doctrine-specific variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnology as an anomalous category requiring special scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Biotech patents in the dataset were adjudicated successfully for patentees only 8% of the time and were more likely to be invalidated or found not infringed than other technologies; this anomaly may stem from selection, functional claiming, notable cases (e.g., Myriad), or changes in patentability standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat biotech results as a puzzle warranting targeted case studies and expanded samples; consider recent doctrinal shifts and landmark invalidations when interpreting aggregate biotech outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations due to missing industry/technology classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors lack technology and industry classifications for all lawsuits filed and settled before dispositive motions; this limits their ability to investigate selection in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document classification coverage and consider possibles biases introduced by unclassified settled cases; prioritize collecting classification data for settled suits in future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting interim wins that likely involve settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost 90% of patentee interim wins in the dataset involve cases that have a termination date in Lex Machina, which likely indicates settlements; counting these as wins may misrepresent merits outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish interim wins that end in settlement from those that remain pending; when possible, separate 'interim win with settlement' from 'interim win proceeding to adjudication' in analyses.
